title: Architecture standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance, and ADRs
author: Ava Chen
content:
Overview

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's architecture and standards across API design, coding practices, infrastructure (IaC and networking), model-serving, observability, and performance. It also indexes active Decision Records (ADRs) that have shaped these standards. The goal is to provide a single reference for engineering teams to build production-grade inference services that are secure, observable, performant, and maintainable.

Scope
- Applies to all public and internal services that implement Redwood's inference, routing, or control-plane functionality.
- Includes hosted API endpoints, Dedicated and Private deployment artifacts, ingestion/transform services, and operator tooling.

Principles
1) Developer ergonomics: standards should reduce cognitive load and speed onboarding.
2) Production-first: defaults must favor safe, observable, and cost-conscious production behavior.
3) Compatability & stability: backwards-compatible API versioning and clear deprecation windows.
4) Measurable SLOs: every service must declare SLOs and a monitoring dashboard.
5) Security by default: least privilege networking and robust secret management.

API Standards
Purpose: Ensure consistent client experience and safe evolution of endpoints.
- API types supported: REST+JSON for public control-plane APIs, gRPC for internal high-throughput service-to-service RPCs, and streaming (Server-Sent Events / WebSockets) for response streaming.
- Versioning: Use explicit major versions in the path (/v1/...) for breaking changes. Backwards-incompatible changes require ADR and a 90-day deprecation policy for hosted endpoints.
- Authentication & authorization: All endpoints must accept OAuth2 bearer tokens or mTLS for internal services. Public API keys must be rate-limited and scoped.
- Error model: HTTP errors must use structured JSON: {"code": "string", "message": "string", "details": []}. Use 4xx for client errors and 5xx for transient server errors. Include a machine-readable error_code for automated handling.
- Request/Response contracts: Prefer explicit schemas (OpenAPI v3) stored alongside code. Use strict JSON schema validation at the API edge.
- Pagination: cursor-based pagination (cursor, limit) for large result sets. Avoid offset where possible.
- Idempotency: Mutating POST endpoints that may be retried should accept an idempotency-key header.
- Rate limiting: Per-API route configs with default quotas (e.g., 100 requests/min for free tier). Expose headers X-RateLimit-* on responses.
- Telemetry: Every API handler must emit request-level spans and metrics (latency, request_count, error_count).

Coding Standards
- Languages & style: Follow language-native style guides. Required linter configs: ESLint (JS/TS), rubocop (Ruby), gofmt + golangci-lint (Go), black + flake8 (Python).
- Dependency management: Pin transitive dependencies via lockfiles. Dependency updates must pass CI security scans and performance benchmarks for model-serving code paths.
- Tests: Minimum coverage requirement for new services is 60% unit coverage; critical runtime components require 80%+ and regression tests for latency-critical code.
- CI: All PRs must run unit tests, linting, security scans (Snyk or equivalent), and a lightweight integration smoke test. PRs that change model-serving kernels or batching logic require a perf gate run (see performance standards).
- Secrets: No secrets in code. Use the company vault (KMS-backed) via the secrets injector for runtime.
- APIs: Use typed interfaces and DTOs for public contracts. Avoid ad-hoc dicts/objects crossing service boundaries.

Infrastructure Standards (IaC & Networking)
- IaC: Terraform is the canonical IaC tool. Modules must be published to the internal registry with semantic versioning. Do not apply manual changes in production; use CI-driven applies with plan approval.
- Environment separation: Distinct accounts/projects for dev/stage/prod, with VPC-level isolation. Network peering must be documented and authorized.
- Tagging: All cloud resources must include tags: team, owner, cost_center, environment.
- Secrets & KMS: Customer keys for Private deployments must integrate with customer KMS/HSM. Platform secrets must be stored in the company vault with RBAC policies.
- Capacity & autoscaling: Default autoscaling policies should aim for <70% average utilization in normal traffic with capacity buffers for bursts.
- Observability hooks: Provision log exports, metrics exporters, and tracing sidecars in IaC modules by default.

Model-Serving Standards
- Model versioning: Every model artifact has a semantic version and manifest describing architecture, tokenizer, quantization profile, and compatible runtime kernel versions.
- Pinning & rollouts: Customer-facing routes should pin model versions by default. Use canary rollouts (5% -> 25% -> 100%) with automatic rollback on quality/perf regressions.
- Quantization & precision: Quantization profiles are stored as artifacts. Runtime chooses quantization based on ADR recommendations and workload profiles; changes require regression evals.
- Batching & KV caching: Prefer dynamic continuous batching; defaults: max_batch_size 32, batch_timeout_ms 15. KV cache policy: per-session TTL 300s by default with LRU eviction.
- Kernel selection & optimization: Runtime must expose a compatible kernel matrix; switch decisions should be codified and backed by perf benchmarks.
- Fallbacks: Implement automatic fallback to lower-fidelity models or region variants under capacity pressure with clear audit logs.

Observability Standards
- Metrics: Export Prometheus-compatible metrics. Required service metrics: requests_total, requests_error_total, request_latency_seconds_bucket, model_inference_time_seconds, gpu_utilization_percent, batch_sizes_histogram.
- Tracing: Use OpenTelemetry. Instrument request paths end-to-end, including model runtime and network hops. Sample rates: default 0.1 for production; 1.0 for canary rollouts.
- Logging: JSON structured logs with fields: timestamp, level, service, trace_id, span_id, request_id, user_id (when available), message. Avoid PII in logs.
- Dashboards & SLOs: Each service must have a dashboard with key metrics and SLO widgets. Baseline SLOs: API availability 99.95% (monthly), inference p99 latency targets (see Performance).
- Alerts: Alert on SLO burn-rate >1.5 for 1h, error rate spikes >5% above baseline, and resource exhaustion (GPU memory >90% for >5m). Alert routing to on-call platform with runbook links.

Performance Standards
- Latency targets (production hosted API default):
  - p50 < 40ms (control-plane API paths)
  - p95 < 150ms
  - p99 < 400ms
- Inference SLOs (per-model class):
  - Small models (<6B): p99 < 200ms, throughput up to 600 tokens/s per A100-equivalent GPU
  - Medium models (6B-30B): p99 < 800ms, throughput up to 200 tokens/s per A100-equivalent GPU
  - Large models (>30B): p99 < 2000ms (where applicable), throughput depends on quantization and sequence length
- Batching guidance: Dynamic batching preferred. Target average batch size >= 8 for high-throughput endpoints. Monitor latency tail for batching adverse effects.
- Benchmarking: Use the benchmarking-and-perf-suite with representative workloads. Any change to runtime kernels, quantization, or batching policies must run a standardized perf suite (latency and cost-per-token) and publish results.

Decision Records (ADRs) Index
- ADR-2024-01: Standardize on REST+gRPC split for public vs. internal APIs - Owner: Jonah Kim - 2024-02-12 - Rationale: clarity for client contracts and higher throughput for internal services.
- ADR-2025-03: Default quantization profiles and rollback policy - Owner: Priya Kapoor - 2025-06-04 - Rationale: Balance cost and quality; require regression evals.
- ADR-2026-02: Batching defaults and continuous-batching runtime design - Owner: Luis Martinez - 2026-01-15 - Rationale: Improve overall cluster throughput while preserving latency SLOs.
(See each ADR page for full decision text, alternatives considered, and metrics used.)

Governance & Ownership
- Standards owners: Architecture & Standards (primary), Eng-Serving-Runtime (model-serving specifics), Eng-Infra (IaC/networking), Eng-SRE (SLOs and runbooks).
- Change process: Significant changes (API breaking, infra network topology, model-serving kernel changes) require an ADR, a perf/security review, and cross-team reviewers.
- Review cadence: Annual review of standards; ad-hoc updates when major platform changes occur.
